Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Record revealed Freddie Mercury’s naturalisation certificate Freddie Mercury was naturalised as a British citizen in 1969. This record tells the story of how he emigrated from Zanzibar to the UK and became a rock music icon. Images Image 1 of 3 Freddie Mercury naturalisation certificate page one, 1969. Catalogue reference: HO 334/1421/117889 Transcript HO 334/1421/117889 117889 Home Office Form R1 (Second Copy) B. 211808 British Nationality Act 1948, Section 6 (1) Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1962, Section 12 (2) Application for registration as a citizen of the United Kingdom and colonies made by a British Subject or Citizen of the Republic of Ireland on the ground of ordinary residence or crown service Caution: to give false information on this form purposely or recklessly is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment (British Nationality Act 1948, Section 28 (1)). I, Frederick/Farrokh BULSARA of 22 Gladstone [Avenue], Feltham, [Middlesex] am of full age and capacity and was born at Zanaibar (Tanzania) on 5th September 1946 My father’s full name is Bomi Bulsara and he was born at Bulsar, [British] India on 14th December 1908 I am single (married) (a widower) (a widow) (divorced from my wife/husband) My (wife’s) (husband’s) full name (is) was…. And (she) (he) was born at … on… I am (a) a citizen of the following country or countries mentioned in section 1(3) of the British Nationality Act 1948, that is to say Zanzibar (Tanzania). (a) I am ordinarily resident in the United Kingdom (a) I have been ordinarily resident in the United Kingdom and colonies during the last five years as follows: 19 Hamilton Close, Feltham, [Middlesex] from 4-5-64 to 31-8-64 122 Hamilton Close, Feltham, [Middlesex] from 1-9-64 to 28-10-64 22 Gladstone [Avenue], Feltham, [Middlesex] from 29-10-64 to present day PTO Image 2 of 3 Freddie Mercury naturalisation certificate page two, 1969. Catalogue reference: HO 334/1421/117889 Transcript 8. The special circumstances in which I desire that the period of ordinary residence of Crown service shorter than five years which is mentioned in paragraph 7 above should be accepted are as follows:…. 9. I (have not) previously renounced or been deprived of citizenship of the United Kingdon and Colonies. [If the applicant has renounced citizenship of the United Kingdom and colonies, here state the date on which the declaration of renunciation was made; and if the applicant has been deprived of citizenship, state the date on which, and the authority by whom, the order of deprivation was made. 10. I hereby apply to be registered as a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies. [The application must be signed in the presence of one of the persons specified in the Appendix to the Instructions.] I, Frederick/Farrokh Bulsara so solemnly and sincerely declare that the foregoing particulars stated in this application are true and I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true. (Signature of applicant) F. Bulsara Made and subscribed this 21st Day of March 1969 Before me D S Mahany at Feltham (signed) D S Mahany [Here state whether Commissioner of Oaths, Justice of the Peace, Notary Public or other authorised person specified in the Appendix to the Instructions] A commissioner of oaths PLEASE DO NOT WRITE ANYTHING BELOW THIS LINE The above named applicant has been registered as a citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies [signed] B Pinsent. 2 [June] 1969 Nationality Division, Home Office, London Image 3 of 3 Freddie Mercury in concert at Slane Castle, County Meath, Ireland, 1986. Copyright: Carol Lee / Alamy Why this record matters Date 2 June 1969 Catalogue reference HO 334/1421/117889 Freddie Mercury (1946–1991) is known to millions as the lead singer of the rock band Queen. He is widely celebrated for his powerful vocals and songwriting talent. Freddie was born Farrokh Bulsara in 1946 in Zanzibar, then a British Protectorate in the Indian Ocean just off the coast of East Africa. He and his family arrived in Feltham, West London in October 1964. Zanzibar had been a British Protectorate since 1890. It was a key centre of trade for spices, in particular cloves, nutmeg, pepper and cinnamon. Under the Zanzibar Act, passed by the UK government in December 1963, the territory was no longer part of the British Empire. Zanzibar became a constitutional monarchy (in which the monarch is head of state but the country is governed by elected officials) within the Commonwealth under the Sultan of Zanzibar. A month later, the Sultan was overthrown during the Zanzibar Revolution and a republic was established. In April 1964 the Republic of Zanzibar joined with Tanganyika, the mainland, and was known thereafter as Tanzania. Freddie and his family were among a number of British colonial staff and their families who left Zanzibar in the aftermath of the revolution. Settling in Feltham, Freddie enrolled in the graphic art and design course at the Ealing Technical College and School of Art (now part of the University of West London). In 1969 Freddie graduated college and became a British citizen by naturalisation. This is the legal process by which a person changes their nationality. To do this, he had to complete this form detailing personal information including his full name, birthplace, residence, and father's name. The form was then approved by the Home Office. The National Archives holds most of the surviving paperwork for successful naturalisations , up until 1986, including Freddie's. In the early 1970s, Freddie sang in bands in London. He became friends with Brian May and Roger Taylor, forming Queen in 1970. Freddie changed his name by deed poll at around this time. He appears to have opted not to enrol (make public record) this change of name with the High Court, so there is no permanent record of this in the public records. This is common, as enrolling a change of name by deed poll was more expensive and not a legal requirement. Queen broke through in Britain in 1974. Their popularity soared with the release of Bohemian Rhapsody in October 1975, which stayed at number one for nine weeks. By the early 1980s, Queen were drawing enormous crowds to their elaborately staged concerts. The band appeared at Live Aid in 1985 with Freddie’s spectacular performance going on to be a key cultural moment in musical history. The band continued to record and release music throughout the 1980s. On 23 November 1991 Freddie announced that he had been diagnosed with AIDS. He died from complications arising from his illness the following day. Freddie was 45 years old. Queen continued to release music after his death and his voice was still featuring in their work as late as 1995. In 2022, the US Library of Congress included Bohemian Rhapsody in the National Recording Registry. It is catalogued as: ‘an over the top musical thrill ride whose six minutes contained more technology-stretching bravado than most bands’ entire careers.’ View record details Discover highlights from the collection Explore the collection : Migration and citizenship Explore the collection : Postwar (1945–present) Help us improve this website Complete our short survey (opens in new tab) Back to top The National Archives Kew , Richmond TW9 4DU Follow us on social media X (formerly Twitter) YouTube Facebook Flickr Instagram Quick links About us Contact us News Blogs Podcasts Image library Press room Jobs British citizenship services Historical Manuscripts Commission Other websites UK Government Web Archive Legislation.gov.uk Find Case Law The Gazette The National Archives Trust Friends of The National Archives National Archives Design System Sign up to our emails Hear about our latest news, stories from the collection and priority booking for events. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Focus on IVF and reproductive technology in the archive About this image A close up of a diagram explaining the fertilisation process. Catalogue reference: FD 7/2308 During its development, many considered in vitro fertilisation (IVF) unethical. Records at The National Archives highlight how this view has changed over time and brings to light the people who fought for, and against, its use. Author Dr Laura Robson-Mainwaring Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist – Modern Health On this page Louise Brown: A glimmer of hope Filming the first IVF birth Developing IVF A new technology raises new questions Voices from the public: Fear and hope A new world The legacy of IVF Louise Brown: A glimmer of hope In July 1978, the world witnessed a medical milestone: the birth of Louise Brown, the first baby conceived through in vitro fertilisation (IVF). The technique, developed by Patrick Steptoe, Robert Edwards, and Jean Purdy, involves fertilising an egg outside the body before transferring the embryo to the uterus. The success of this process marked the beginning of a scientific and social transformation. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, well before Louise’s birth, the press began sharing concerns about IVF. UK Government records, held by The National Archives, show that this publicity alarmed the public and many people were concerned about the ethical implications of IVF. For couples experiencing infertility, however, these medical developments created hope and presented a potential path to parenthood. Image 1 of 2 Newspaper clipping from The Guardian for an article titled 'Time ripe for first tube baby', 4 January 1972. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Image 2 of 2 Newspaper clipping from the Daily Sketch for an article titled 'Doctor in plea for test tube baby inquiry', 2 November 1970. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 From our collection MH 166/928 Title Government consultation, correspondence and minutes of meetings regarding IVF Date 1965–1973 At this time, advances in reproductive medicine, IVF, surrogacy, and later gene editing, created profound ethical questions such as: When does human life begin? Is it acceptable to manipulate embryos? Who holds parental rights? How should society guard against exploitation and unequal access? Today, IVF is a well-accepted part of reproductive healthcare. In 2023 alone, one in every 32 births in the UK were the result of IVF treatment, which is equivalent to one child in every classroom. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, however, the technology was unprecedented and considered controversial. Filming the first IVF birth A file (catalogue reference: INF 12/13/1399) from the Central Office of Information (COI) shows the widespread public interest surrounding Louise Brown’s birth. Ministers decided to commission the COI to produce an official film. This footage would assess the baby’s condition at birth and create a historical record of IVF’s use. Lesley Brown (Louise’s mother) also decided to sell her story exclusively to Associated Newspapers Ltd (Daily Mail) before entering Oldham General District Hospital. This meant, frustratingly for the Department of Health and Social Security (DHSS), that there would be a 28–day embargo (waiting period) before any footage they recorded could be shared publicly. On Monday 24 July, the DHSS asked the COI’s Films Division to be ready to film the birth of the world’s first IVF baby. Our records show that, throughout the day, COI stayed in touch with the Regional Health Authority and Steptoe, who confirmed that the birth would not happen before Thursday evening. On that basis, the film crew was told to stand down for 24 hours, but everything changed the next morning. At 11:30 am on Tuesday 25 July, Tony Buckingham from the Regional Health Authority phoned with an urgent warning that the birth could happen at any moment. As a result, the COI sent the film crew racing to Oldham. Final filming rights were secured, including from Mrs Brown at 11:15 pm. Just 15 minutes later at 11:30 pm, the caesarean section began. Louise was born at 11:47 pm, weighing 5 lbs 12 oz. The footage is preserved at the British Film Institute (BFI) and made available online by Wellcome Collection. Open transcript TEST TUBE BABY 24 MINUTE NEWS ITEM At 23.47 BST on 25 July 1978 a unique baby was born in Britain - the result of a "test-tube" fertilisation. Louise Joy Brown, the 51b 12oz daughter of Mr and Mrs Brown of Bristol, was delivered safely by Caesarian section by Patrick Steptoe Esq FRCS FRCOG, Honarary Consultant Gynaecologist at the Oldham General Hospital near Manchester. He was assisted by Dr John Webster MB ChB MRCOG, by Dr Finlay Campbell FSARCS DA (Anaesthetist), Theatre Sister Astel SRN and Sister Marshall SRN, Dr. Hilson MAMB BChir FRCP(L) FRCP(E) MRCS DCH (Consultant Paediatrician). Also present at the birth was Dr Robert Edwards DSc PhD, the Cambridge physiologist whose 20 years of research led to the successful fertilisation. The historic birth was commented on by Dr Edwards as "A close collaboration between scientist and doctor". Length: 86 1/2 ft 26.33 metres Time: 2 mins 24 secs at 24 fps 2 mins 17 secs at 25 fps Sales enquiries please to: Sales Unit Film and Television Division Central Office of Information Hercules Road London SEl Tel. 01-928 2345, Ext 227 or 224 Telex 91544 CENTROFORM LDN Memorandum showing the description of the two minute news reel produced by the COI at the birth of Louise Brown, 1978. There was a longer (15 minute) clinical version , narrated by Steptoe. Please note, both videos contain graphic depictions of a medical procedure (a cesarean section). Catalogue reference: INF 12/1399 From our collection INF 12/1399 Title Central Office of Information's notes on their film coverage of the birth of the first 'test tube' baby Date July–October 1978 Developing IVF In the early 1970s, Edwards and Steptoe were developing techniques that would eventually lead to Louise’s birth. Records of the Medical Research Council (MRC) show that they applied for funding in May 1971 but were turned down on ethical grounds. For most of the 1970s, the MRC viewed IVF as too experimental, too risky, and too poorly supported by clinical infrastructure to justify funding . The MRC instead encouraged them to undertake studies on animals. Open transcript 2. Long-term support declined (a) Dr R.G. Edwards (University of Cambridge) and Mr P.C. Steptoe (consultant gynaecologist, Oldham): application for long-term support for studies on human reproduction (MRC 71/239). The application was declined because of serious doubts about the ethical aspects of the proposed investigations, especially those relating to the implantation in women of oocytes fertilized in vitro which were considered premature. Dr Edwards should, however, be encouraged, without commitment, to undertake studies of the type proposed in animals. Medical Research Council Meeting ‘Long-term support denied’, 20 May 1971, Catalogue reference: FD 13/171 From our collection FD 13/171 Title Notes from the Medical Research Council's Meeting Date May 1971 Despite the rejection, their research continued with private funding. After the safe and successful birth of the first IVF baby, Louise, the MRC became a strong supporter of IVF research. This opened the door to mainstream clinical development and a state-focused examination of the ethical issues involved. A new technology raises new questions The Committee of Inquiry into Human Fertilisation and Embryology, chaired by the moral philosopher Dame Mary Warnock, was established in 1982 by the DHSS. Its members included doctors, scientists, a psychologist, and faith representatives, reflecting the scientific, social, and moral issues at stake. Together, they discussed whether IVF should be permitted, and if so, how it should be regulated. They also discussed the moral status of an embryo created in a laboratory and whether the state should regulate who could access IVF. The fundamental moral objection to IVF was that, for the procedure to be successful, several eggs must be fertilised, meaning that some embryos are likely to be destroyed or discarded during the process. This is because not all embryos develop successfully, so multiple embryos are created to increase the chances of a successful pregnancy. Despite this, their final report approved the use of IVF, with some limitations, and recommended the creation of a voluntary licensing authority, an independent body that would monitor IVF clinics to ensure ethical standards were being followed. It also concluded that commercial surrogacy was unethical, meaning the carrier of an embryo cannot be paid by the parent(s) for carrying their baby. Additionally, the committee suggested that human embryos used in research should not be kept alive in vitro beyond 14 days as this would be unethical. Although the report was signed by all members, differing views on when life begins led to expressions of dissent within the report that, they claimed, ‘ reflected the range of views in society ’. The report went on to lay the basis for the regulatory framework established by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990. Open transcript MRC/RCOG Voluntary Licensing Authority for Human In Vitro Fertilisation and Embryology. Guidelines for both clinical and research applications of Human In Vitro Fertilisation 1985. The Voluntary Licensing Authority (VLA) is jointly sponsored by the Medical Research Council and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists. Guidelines for clinical and research applications for Human In Vitro Fertilisation from the voluntary licensing authority,1985. Catalogue reference: FD 7/3321 From our collection FD 7/3321 Title Reports, notes and correspondence on IVF Date 1986–1989 Voices from the public: Fear and hope Letters from ordinary people, found in the archive, capture the emotional and moral intensity of the public debate around IVF. One correspondent wrote, 'Research babies in bottles’, I’ve never heard of anything so repulsive. Letter from a member of the public to the Secretary of State for Social Services, 2 November 1970., Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 We heartily disapprove of this research, because if nature decides that children should not be born then artificial means should not be used. Imagine a child having to realise he was a test tube child. Letter from a member of the public to the Lord President of the Council, 30 January 1974., Catalogue reference: INF 12/1399 Open transcript February 26th 1967. The Minister of Health Dear Sir In view of the clear admission on ITN news this evening that experiments on human foetuses will be a necessary preliminary to the successful implantation in the womb of eggs fertilised outside the human body, would you kindly give me an answer to the following points: a) do yon personally approve of this technique in making childbirth possible? b) Do you personally consider that there are no ethical objections to the experimentation currently in progress? c) Are National Health and/or University facilities being used for this research? d) Have you power to direct that such experiments cease? e) If so, will you provide the direction the medical profession is seeking, and order an immediate cessation of these activities? You can no doubt deduce my own attitude. Yours sincerely John Wilson (Liberal Prospective Parliamentary Candidate for Hemel Hempstead) Letter from Parliamentary Candidate John Wilson to the Minister of Health, 26 February 1967. Catalogue reference: MH 166/928 Others wrote pleading for access to treatment, revealing the emotional toll of infertility and the personal stakes behind the debates. One couple who had been married for ten years described themselves as living ‘in a hopeless condition’ and asked to ‘participate in this service to humanity… We are willing to accept your terms of payment (whatever it may be).’ Open transcript 12th May ‘73 The Ministry of Health, London Re: Test Tube Babies Sir Recently in one of our local papers we came across one article which has inspired us to write this letter. We are a sterile couple, married for the last ten years: in the 7th year of our married life my Mrs had to undergo an emergency operation. Right phallopean [sic] tube bursted [sic] due to advanced ectopic pregnancy (approx. 2 ½ months). While cutting and clamping the doctors thought it wise to remove cyst from left tube also, however unfortunately the second tube along with cyst was removed, leaving us completely incapable to conceive & in hopeless condition. We accepted the life as if we have lost a limb & are living the life of satisfaction. However when we read the report in the paper that in U.K. you are successful in planting fertilised ovum in the womb and baby could develop thereafter. We have thought it wise to refer this matter to you and we wonder whether we could participate in this service to humanity & be benefited with your success. We are willing to accept your terms of payment etc (whatever it may be). It will be in order to mention here that we are a couple of 35/33 yrs of age (husb/wife) physically fit. Sperm count: 120 million/cc & all other qualities/quantities being above normal: m.c. regular. If you require any certificate or any medical opinion/ questioning to be answered we will be too glad to furnish the same. We hope you will extend you helping hand before we get too old to participate. Sincerely thanking you [signature]. A letter from a couple dealing with fertility challenges to the Ministry of Health, 12 May 1973. Catalogue reference: MH 156/458 Patients of Patrick Steptoe also wrote in his defence. After spotting a local newspaper report in Oldham’s Evening Chronicle suggesting his work was a step toward euthanasia, one woman passionately directed her letter to Prime Minister James Callaghan: Mr Steptoe is my doctor, and I am involved in these ‘experiments’ as they put it…. I have met so many young women in Dr Kershaws Hospital whilst we have been receiving treatment, we all love Mr Steptoe very much indeed, he is our only hope to have a child of our own, he is a kind, considerate and very wonderful man, and all he is trying to do is help us, we have no other hope, at all… It’s a terrible thing to be told you can’t have a child, and then all of a sudden you meet Mr Steptoe and there’s a glimmer of hope. A patient of Dr Steptoe to the Prime Minister James Callaghan, undated letter., Catalogue reference MH 156/458 Open transcript …that a Mr. A Mcgarty was going to ask you to investigate Mr Steptoe’s work, this is why I’m writing to you put ‘our’ side of the story to you as well. I say ‘our’ because I have met so many young women in the Kershaw’s Hospital whilst we have been receiving treatment, we all love Mr Steptoe very much indeed, he is our only hope to have a child of our own, he is a kind, considerate man, and all he is trying to do is help us, we have no other hope, at all. Please, ask your wife her feelings, as a women, I’m sure she’ll understand, it’s a terrible thing to be told you can’t have… Page from multi-page letter from a patient of Dr Steptoe to the Prime Minister James Callaghan, undated letter. Catalogue reference MH 156/458 From our collection MH 156/458 Title Background documents and correspondence on IVF and the birth of Louise Brown Date 1973–1979 Another patient of Steptoe, describing the treatment as her only hope, wrote: If the people objecting to this treatment had experiences the torment and misery of a woman who is unable to conceive I am sure they would look at this matter in a different light. Letter from a patient of Dr Steptoe to her local MP, 22 May 1969., Catalogue reference: FD 9/1430 From our collection FD 9/1430 Title Enquiries from the public on IVF research Date 1969–1973 A new world Following the successful birth of Louise Brown, Steptoe, Edwards and Purdy worked towards founding Bourn Hall, which became the world’s first IVF clinic in 1980. Here, they worked to advance IVF techniques. Around this time, advancements were also happening across the globe, with the world’s second IVF baby being born in October 1978 in Kolkata, India. Image 1 of 2 Extracts of a leaflet for Bourn Hall IVF Clinic, 1985. Catalogue reference: FD 7/3334 Image 2 of 2 The leaflet reads, 'Collecting these samples will be organised by the nursing staff. The results of the hormone investigations will enable the time of ovulation to be accurately predicted. (b) When ovulation is imminent, the wife will be notified that the egg recovery procedure will shortly take place, and she will be prepared for the operation, which is again a laparoscopy technique. Based on the Clinic's work to date, the percentage of eggs recovered is very high. (c) When the time of ovulation is diagnosed, the husband will be asked to attend the Clinic to provide a fresh semen sample, for fertilisation of his wife's egg. The process of fertilisation is carried out in an exceptionally sterile environment and the embryology work of nurturing the embryo to the stage where replacement can be effected takes approximately 3 days. The percentage of eggs successfully fertilised is over 80%. (d) Replacement of the fertilised egg (embryo) will be carried out in the operating theatre, usually without anaesthesia. (e) A period of a few hours rest and medical care will then follow, until the wife is advised she can leave. ... Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 From our collection FD 7/2308 Title Files from the inquiry into Human Fertilisation and Embryology (Warnock Committee). Date 1982–1984 From our collection FD 7/3334 Title Files related to Bourn Hall Clinic, Cambridge. Date 1985–1989 Sadly, Jean Purdy passed away in 1985 after helping to develop and refine the laboratory techniques that made IVF possible. Patrick Steptoe died in 1988, having helped transform fertility treatment through his pioneering work in laparoscopy and IVF alongside Edwards. Their contributions established IVF as a viable medical option for overcoming infertility and offered hope to millions of couples worldwide. Following Steptoe's death, Dame Mary Donaldson, Chair of the Voluntary Licensing Authority, described him as: ... a man of pioneering spirit but also one of great integrity. His death marks the end of an era but his influence will undoubtedly spread into the next. Dame Mary Donaldson to Mrs P Steptoe, 23 March 1988, Catalogue reference: FD 7/3334 Bourn Hall Clinic still operates today, and Steptoe, Edwards, and Purdy’s work continues to have a global impact. The legacy of IVF The archival material surrounding the development of IVF is invaluable for understanding how governments and society responded to the challenges posed by new reproductive technologies. While IVF is not a definitive cure for infertility and does not always succeed, it continues to offer hope to many. This was made possible by the pioneering work of figures such as Steptoe, Edwards, and Purdy, as well as the persistent hope of the hundreds of women involved in their early experiments. nhs.uk Would you like to learn more about IVF? Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Focus on Home front India: Women’s experiences in a Second World War battle zone About this image Manipuri women who appear to be waiting at an airfield to begin work in loading or unloading’. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 A small set of photographs in our collection shows women from Manipur, India at work on an airfield during the Second World War. What was their experience of living on the ‘home front’ at the heart of one of the most brutal battles of the conflict? Author Dr Elizabeth Haines Roles Author Researcher Principal Records Specialist – Empire and Commonwealth On this page Women in a battle zone Experiences of the conflict The war in context Ambiguous legacies Important information ! This article includes references to armed violence, starvation, homelessness and sexual violence. An image of a document contains an ethnic slur. These are included here to accurately represent historical records and people’s past experiences. Women in a battle zone A small number of photographs of the 1944 Siege of Imphal – the capital city of the state of Manipur, North Eastern India – can be found in the records of the Royal Air Force (RAF). A report of around 60 pages, held by The National Archives as AIR 23/1956, focuses on military logistics but also describes the living conditions of those posted there. From our collection AIR 23/1956 Title Narrative on the Siege of Imphal, India, March to June 1944 Date 1945 Members of the British Army, the Indian Army, the RAF and the United States Air Force all found themselves in the city during one of the key battles of the Second World War. The Battle of Imphal was polled (jointly with the nearby battle of Kohima) as 'Britain’s Greatest Battle' by a poll from the National Army Museum in 2013. In the course of the Second World War, the valley had received thousands of exhausted civilian refugees retreating from Burma (present day Myanmar) in early 1942, and had been bombed since December 1942 by the Japanese military. The wider state of Manipur had been partially invaded by the Japanese and subjected to a scorched earth policy by the Allies – the systematic destruction of resources that could later benefit the enemy. In some parts every single building was destroyed. As a frontline of the war, the rice-growing valley became a military camp. North Eastern India received 340,000 Indian troops, 100,000 British troops, 90,000 African troops, 65,000 Chinese troops and 10,000 American troops. The Imphal valley alone at one point held 200,000 troops for 330,000 inhabitants. Over half of the houses owned by Meitei (the Tibeto-Burman people who make up the larger part of the population in the valley) were requisitioned for military purposes. New road infrastructures changed the landscape entirely, and food supplies and labour patterns were transformed. This map printed by the Allied Land Forces South East Asia in 1944 show the movement of the 15th Division of the Japanese Army (in blue) towards and into the Imphal valley between March and June. Catalogue reference: WO 252/1444 The photographs show an airfield where women are working and talking, alongside the soldiers, planes and military technologies supporting an unprecedented jungle warfare campaign. Framed by an unknown photographer, these may be some of a very small number of images that show Manipuri women at work during the conflict. Open transcript Manipuris show a keen interest in long range petrol tanks. Photograph of Manipuri women possibly being shown to lift aircraft petrol tanks. They appear very young, and their clothing and hair suggest that some may be fairly recent brides. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 While the impact of the Second World War on many places around the world has barely been recorded, the longer history of Imphal and Manipur has been politically contested and more closely studied. Historians have used both written sources and oral history accounts to bring better understanding of what that moment meant. In the military report in AIR 23/1956, and in the original captions for the photographs, the women are framed as exotic, attractive and useful to the war effort. Wider sources, however, invite us to consider the experience of the war from women’s own points of view. Experiences of the conflict Japan Lan (Japan War), as it is known in Meitei, was a moment of incredibly rapid change for individuals and society in Manipur. In first-hand accounts and in oral histories that have been collected we can see the ambiguities and contradictions, opportunity and desolation that characterised the experience of living in a battle zone. Many of those in this article come from How Women Remember War, a compilation of oral histories published in 2019 by Leisangthem Gitarani Devi . Witness accounts demonstrate that the war brought violence and fear. The report in AIR 23/1956 mentions that bombing in 1944 killed ‘a certain number of civilian Manipuris’. Wider reports by the colonial administration and oral histories show that bombing by the Japanese destroyed entire residential areas and marketplaces. The only shelters from this threat were trenches with branches and leaves. The plane began bombing the trench … my sister and elder brother were deeper inside. They were buried in the mud. The following morning, they had to be dug out with hands. Yumkhaibam ongbi Manjuri Apart from the danger of being killed by bullets or shells there was also the danger of being bitten by snakes in the trenches. Thokchom Ramani The town of Imphal as seen from the sky in December 1943. This image is part of a series documenting the frontier between British India and Burma, particularly roads, rivers, airfields and other lines of communication. Catalogue reference: CN 1/7 Forests and agricultural land were both requisitioned and destroyed by armed forces on both sides, and food was diverted to the troops. We didn’t have any food. We would often fill our stomachs with water chestnut [from a large lake] when there was no rice available for days … They [the soldiers] burnt all the houses and the granaries. We lost a lot of food grains. We were asked to evacuate our houses. We fled the war for about a year. Pukhrambam Ningol Khwairakpam ongbi Madhumati Several accounts describe how the presence of large numbers of male troops was a threat to women. They [the Allied soldiers] treated children very affectionately. However, at night, they would come asking for women. Women couldn’t venture out at night. Groups of men kept vigil at night with sticks and swords. Thokchom Ramani In the face of all of this, the accounts show that the encounter with military technology was still enthralling. They [aeroplanes] used to fly very, very high like swallows. They would emit smoke in the sky all around, and we would especially watch the trails of smoke. Madhumati For an orphaned Manipuri boy, who later wrote an autobiography, The Second World War in Manipur And My Childhood, it was captivating: Every day and night, thousands of different vehicles, quite strange to this place were ceaselessly coming in, carrying soldiers, guns, technicians... We hardly remembered our personal sorrows in the midst of all that grandeur of war. Khuraijam Nimaicharan Singh In Meitei society in the early 20th century women were important contributors to household income. One major market in Imphal was exclusively run by women vendors. However, the war also shifted the kinds of work that women were likely to be doing. AIR 23/1956 describes women as loading and unloading transport aircraft that were bringing troops and supplies ‘a work in which the cheerful and gaily-clad Manipuri women would laughingly collaborate’. Most accounts agree that labouring work for the Allied armed forces was well-paid, although some women reported being ashamed of taking on this kind of manual labour. Open transcript Dakota aircraft carried a wide variety of equipment to the Imphal Valley. Since all land communications had been cut by the Japanese, no M.T. could reach the garrison, and small vehicles such as jeeps were flown in by transport aircraft. This photograph gives a sense of the airfield as the meeting of military and civilian, with men in uniform loading the plane and women in civilian clothes working in parallel. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 However, women were also involved in heavier labour such as the construction of the the vital all-weather airfield at Imphal. Once the tractor had laid the road, women carried all the stones and mud and many other things for tarring the road. Khuraijam Nimaicharan Singh Koirengei As property was destroyed and their livelihoods disrupted more women took up sex work. [During the war] women couldn’t go out for over two months. They had to stop their businesses in the market. So they started trading their flesh for money… these women would often come back and take care of their children. Yumkhaibam Manjuri The war in context Even these brief extracts describing the effect of the war suggest how Manipuri sources offer a more ambiguous picture of the Allies than we often encounter in the UK. Situating the years 1942 to 1944 in the longer history of the Imphal Valley give a better context to this moment of extreme conflict within the lives of the valley's inhabitants. Manipur was only formally integrated into the British Empire as part of British India less than 50 years before the outbreak of the Second World War. At earlier moments Imphal had been part of the Toungoo Empire, centred around today’s Myanmar. By the time of the Japanese invasion in 1942, Manipuri women had succeeded in turning back British colonial policy twice, in events known in Meitei as Nupi Lan (women’s wars). In 1904 women had successfully protested forced labour that had been imposed as a form of collective punishment. In 1939, at the outbreak of the war, thousands of women had conducted a market boycott to resist the export of rice that was causing famine conditions in Manipur. After several days of protest and enduring armed violence, they succeeded in this too. While these photographs show the women working for the Allied forces, it might be wrong to interpret that they supported the Allies' cause. Open transcript In dry weather the difficulties of rain and mud are replaced by the dust hazard. At Kangla, a fair-weather strip near Imphal, hundreds of transport aircraft landed daily, and at times the dust raised an impenetrable fog. The photo gives a good impression of conditions. In the foreground, are Manipuri women who are employed by the Air Forces and by the Army. Manipuri women who appear to be waiting at an airfield to begin work in loading or unloading, standing close to aeroplanes described elsewhere as like ‘swallows’. Catalogue reference: AIR 23/1956 Some Indians in the 1940s saw co-operation with the Japanese as a faster route to self-governance than loyalty to the British. Historians have shown that some Manipuris joined the Indian National Army, and fought on the side of the Japanese at Imphal. Intense propaganda campaigns were made by both sides. Records from the British administration and Japanese forces show that they were both keen to keep the people at the centre of the destruction in the Imphal Valley on ‘their side’. Commit no offences whatever against them… The Indians have for years been awaiting their delivery at our hands. The Commander of the Japanese forces to his troops at Imphal. Catalogue reference: CAB 106/50 A letter from the representative of the British Indian government in Manipur describes the destruction of Manipuri communities taking place in Imphal in 1944: If many more of them see their houses, property and food destroyed by us, they can hardly be expected to remain enthusiastically pro-British. E. F. Lydall, Political Agent in Manipur, 16 April 1944. Catalogue reference: WO 203/3200 He describes the effect of the Allied ‘Scorched Earth’ policy on the Imphal valley and asks for more attention from the military to the living conditions of the communities that have been displaced. Open transcript Economically, the piling up of villagers in increasing crowded conditions presents an immediate problem and the destruction of paddy and the prospect of considerable areas of paddy land being cultivated inadequately or not at all is one which forces one to envisage famine conditions in the devastated and evacuated areas. These so far are approximately all areas near the foothills to the north, north-east, south-east and south of the valley, as well as the area south of Bishenpur. Politically, the Manipuris have already had their confidence severely shaken by the Japanese invasion of their country, great play having been made in the last few years that they must not mind giving up their houses to the military who were here to defend them from the enemy. If many more of them see their houses, property and food destroyed by us, they can hardly be expected to remain enthusiastically pro-British. Letter from E. F. Lydall, the Political Agent (representative of the British Indian government) in Manipur, 16 April 1944. Catalogue reference: WO 203/3200 The tensions of being at the site of conflict between empires are reflected in oral history. Some accounts from men and women speak favourably of their relationships with the Japanese invaders. Ambiguous legacies The extent of the destruction caused by both Allies and Japanese mean that for many Manipuris, the surrender of the Japanese forces did not mean a ‘win’. The end of the war left the Imphal valley entirely transformed. Record revealed Japanese Instrument of Surrender, 1945 After six years of brutal global conflict, this document marked the end of the Second World War. Some eventually received compensation to rebuild with, first from the Manipur government, and later from the independent Indian government. Other changes were permanent. Still a borderland territory, the new infrastructure meant that post-war Imphal was far less rural. It was now at the centre of a road network connecting India and Burma. The strengthening of the British presence and social change had meant a weakening of the Manipuri royalty. In 1947 Manipur became the first princely state in Asia to have democratic government. Separatist movements remain active in Manipur, which has been governed under a state of emergency since it was declared a ‘disturbed territory’ by the Indian government in 1958. The fairly rapid retreat of the Allies left weapons behind, and the roads network into northwest Burma became and remains an important route for drug-smuggling. For most of the 80 years since the Second World War, women have continued to survive alongside armed conflict, most recently insurgents and counter-insurgency forces. Some of the Manipuri women whose oral histories of the Second World War have been recorded were among the Meira Paibi movement (women bearing flaming torches). They have been campaigning for citizens’ rights, particularly protection for women against violence, through night-patrols and protests since the 1970s. The images in AIR 23/1956, far more than the words in the report, open up reflection on how ‘Britain’s Greatest Battle’ was lived on the front-line by the women who found themselves caught up in that short moment, and in its legacy. They point to the ongoing work that is needed to build a fuller understanding of the impact of the Second World War in India, and of the complex legacies it has had in South Asia and beyond. Further reading Leishangthem Gitarani Devi (2019), How Women Remember War: Unearthing Memories of the Second World War in Manipur , Zubaan Publishers Pvt. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection The story of James Stagg: The weatherman who turned the tide of D-Day The success of D-Day depended on the accurate forecasting of weather conditions by a team of meteorologists, led by James Stagg. Our records describe the pressure they were under and how they came to play a crucial role in the largest seaborn invasion in history. About this image The Allied leaders preparing their plans for the invasion of Europe. General Dwight D. Eisenhower is sat in the middle. Catalogue reference: INF 2/11 On this page Operation Overlord Stagg and his career Gathering the data Deciding when to launch Stormy weather D-Day Operation Overlord The D-Day landings, officially known as Operation Overlord, remain one of the most significant military operations in history. On 6 June 1944, Allied forces from several nations landed on the beaches of northern France. Here they opened a new front against Nazi Germany, which helped to bring about the end of the Second World War in Europe. While the scale of the operation was unprecedented, its success depended on more than military planning and manpower. Crucially, it relied on the accurate interpretation of weather conditions by a team of meteorologists led by Group Captain James Stagg. Their forecasts played a vital role in determining when the invasion could take place. Records at The National Archives, including reports and the weather forecasts they produced, detail their crucial work. Stagg and his career Born and educated in Scotland, Stagg earned his degrees from the University of Edinburgh before beginning his professional career as a science teacher. At the age of 24, he joined the British Meteorological Office (now the Met Office) as an assistant. During his time at the Meteorological Office, which was operated by the Air Ministry, the government department responsible for the Royal Air Force, he also served as a Senior Technical Officer. In 1932, he participated in a Royal Society polar expedition of Arctic Canada. Before the outbreak of the Second World War, he was appointed Superintendent of Kew Observatory – then the central observatory for the Meteorological Office. At the start of the Second World War, Stagg served as a civilian member of the meteorological service. In April 1944, he was granted an Emergency Commission as a Group Captain in the Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve. He was subsequently appointed Chief Meteorological Officer at the Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force (SHAEF) – the military command responsible for planning and executing the Allied invasion of northwest Europe. Here, Stagg led the team responsible for providing weather forecasts to senior Allied commanders including General Dwight D. Eisenhower who was the Supreme Allied Commander of SHAEF. Group Captain James Stagg, from the Imperial War Museum collection . Gathering the data Weather forecasting was considered a matter of national security during the Second World War, so much so that public weather forecasts were suspended for the duration of the conflict. This did not mean, however, that meteorological observations stopped. Accurate weather data remained essential for military planning, particularly in the lead-up to Operation Overlord. In an age before satellite technology, gathering this information was a challenging and complex task. In early 1944, a joint British-American Meteorological Section was established specifically to provide weather forecasts for D-Day. The team collected data from several sources. During the week before the planned invasion on 5 June, eight British and American weather ships were stationed at designated locations across the Atlantic to monitor and report atmospheric conditions. In addition, the Royal Air Force carried out a series of meteorological reconnaissance flights, although the information obtained from these missions was sometimes considered unreliable. Together with weather reports from the west coast of Ireland, these observations provided a broad picture of conditions across the North Atlantic. The data was then analysed by Stagg and his team who interpreted the forecasts. They then supplied senior SHAEF commanders with the information they needed to determine whether weather conditions were suitable for launching the invasion. Open transcript Chart of Weather in the Northern Hemisphere Morning of Monday 5th June 1944. GENERAL INFERENCE: A depression centred near the Shetlands is drifting northeast and beginning to ease up. There will be strong to gale force west to northwest winds in Shetland at first, moderating steadily. It will be mainly cloudy throughout the British Isles with showers in Scotland, N. England and N. Ireland and scattered showers further south at first; later showers are expected to die out in England, Ireland and S. Scotland. It will be rather cool in the South, cool in the North. FURTHER OUTLOOK: Rain spreading into W. Ireland, and W. Scotland later tomorrow afternoon moving east. Gale warning in operation in districts 13A, 13B. Time of issue 0800 4.6.44 and in districts 11,15, and 16 at 13.55 4.6.44. Weather forecast for the Northern Hemisphere on the morning of Monday 5 June 1944, the planned date for D-Day. Catalogue reference: AIR 37/1124A Deciding when to launch At the end of the war, a report was written examining the meteorological factors that influenced the choice of date for the Allied invasion. It concluded that the ideal conditions for the operation would have included light or calm winds and clear visibility unaffected by fog, mist, or haze. The report acknowledged, however, that such conditions were rarely achievable. As it noted: in English weather, even English summer weather, it was clearly impracticable to set up an ideal set of conditions and defer the assault until this set of conditions was obtained. Catalogue reference: CAB 106/976 In addition to military and political considerations, planners also had to account for the timing of high and low tides, as well as levels of natural illumination influenced by twilight and the phase and position of the moon. Consequently, the Allies agreed upon a set of minimum acceptable meteorological conditions under which the invasion could proceed. These criteria ultimately formed the basis for the decision to launch Operation Overlord on 6 June 1944. Even with agreed thresholds in place, however, the task of producing and interpreting weather forecasts was far from straightforward. The decision depended entirely on predictions of rapidly changing conditions, placing enormous pressure on those responsible for advising the Allied command. The intensity of these discussions is reflected in documents preserved at The National Archives. Open transcript The conference room was ANCXF Mess Room in Southwick House, a large room with a table at one end and easy chairs at the other; walls on three sides lined with bookcases, most of which were empty except for a certain number of books from the Navigation School at PORTSMOUTH which had been using the house for some time since their own headquarters was blitzed. The conference table was not used; the meetings were informal, those present using the easy chairs and the weather exposition being given at the very start. The weather situation was dealt with on each occasion by the Senior Meteorologist – Group Captain STAGG – who was accompanied by Commander PLEMING R.N. and Colonel YATES, U.S. Army Air Corps. Prior to this series the previous meetings to consider the weather had been held at SHAEF and on Monday, 29th May, 1944 Group Captain STAGG had given an optimistic long-range forecast with a considerable degree of confidence. However, on the Saturday night he had a different tale to tell. The long period of settled conditions was breaking up and the outlook for D-Day and the succeeding days was now most unpromising; in fact, the type of weather to be expected was such that made forecasting for more than 24 hours a very hazardous undertaking. D-Day weather report. Catalogue reference: AIR 37/1124A Stormy weather With the invasion initially scheduled for 5 June, a series of meetings began on the evening of Saturday 3 June to determine whether the operation should proceed as planned or be postponed. Forecasting conditions had been relatively uncomplicated up to that point, but by the weekend the weather had deteriorated significantly. Stagg later recalled that the changing conditions made reliable prediction much more difficult. As forecasts continued to be updated throughout the weekend, it became increasingly clear that the invasion could not go ahead on 5 June, as planned. Senior commanders met repeatedly to review the latest meteorological assessments and consider their implications. During a crucial meeting on the night of 4 June, Stagg and his team advised that a brief improvement in conditions was likely on 6 June. On the basis of this forecast, General Dwight D. Eisenhower made the decision to proceed, reportedly remarking: 'Well boys, there it is, I don't see how we can possibly do anything else.' Open transcript 2100, Sunday, 4th June. Supreme Commander’s meeting. Since the statement made before the meeting on Saturday evening, there have been some rapid and unexpected developments in the weather situation over the Atlantic. A front from one of the deep depressions in the northwest Atlantic has moved much farther south than was expected and is now traversing the Channel areas. It is almost over Portsmouth now and will clear the eastern Channel at least on the English side overnight. When that front has passed there will be an interval of fair conditions which, from the evidence we now have, should last until at least dawn on Tuesday. Wind speeds by Monday evening should decrease to Force 3-4 on the French Channel coasts and cloud will become mainly less than 5/10, with base 2-3000 ft. After that interval, lasting till Tuesday morning, cloud will probably increase to 8/10-10/10 from the west during Tuesday afternoon and will continue so overnight Tuesday. From a time on Wednesday which cannot be defined from present information, mainly cloudy conditions will continue; but there should be some intervals of broken cloud. In this period from Wednesday to Friday, there will probably be intervals of 10/10ths cloud with base at 1000 feet; these overcast intervals of low cloud may be expected to last 4-6 hours at a time. Report on the meteorological implications in the selection of the day for D-Day. Catalogue reference: CAB 106/976 Stagg later recorded the events in his diary. He recalled Eisenhower telling him: Well, Stagg, I promise you now that if this forecast of yours comes off, I'll give each of you a bottle of whiskey. General Dwight D. Eisenhower, Catalogue reference: CAB 106/976 D-Day In his entry for 6 June, Stagg wrote that he rose at 5am and reported to his post, where Admiral Creasy, Chief of Staff to Admiral Sir Bertram Ramsay, Commander of the Allied Naval Expeditionary Force, greeted him with the words: 'You must feel a tremendous load off your shoulders, Stagg. Anyway, you can feel proud of your forecast.' Soon afterwards, the invasion began. The forecasts had been made, the decision had been taken, and the success of the operation would now depend on events unfolding across the English Channel. In the early hours of 6 June 1944, more than 150,000 Allied troops landed by sea and air onto five beaches in Normandy, France. While the weather conditions were not perfect, it was better than the previous day – Stagg's judgement had proved correct. The Allied troops were able to make good progress, despite heavy casualties. By the end of the day, they had taken all the beaches they had set out to hold. Eisenhower, who went on to become the 34th president of the United States, would later commend James Stagg's team, writing: I wish you to express my appreciation to the members of your section and the meteorological personnel of subordinate and associated agencies whose combined goodwill and co-operation contributed so much to the final results. General Dwight D. Eisenhower, Catalogue reference: AIR 73/8 Open transcript SECRET SUPREME HEADQUARTERS ALLIED EXPEDITIONARY FORCE Office of the Supreme Commander 28 June 1944 SUBJECT: Commendation TO: Group Captain J.M. Stagg, OBE, Chief, Meteorological Section, G-3 Division, SHAEF. I desire to commend you for the skilful operation of the meteorological services in support of the ‘OVERLORD’ assault on the Continent of EUROPE. I wish you to express my appreciation to the members of your section and the meteorological personnel of subordinate and associated agencies whose combined goodwill and co-operation contributed so much to the final results. Through the months preceding D day your tireless efforts, good judgement, skill and sound leadership resulted in the development of a procedure capable of utilizing the talents and facilities of both nations and all services in a unified manner. I have been particularly impressed with the sound approach made by you to the difficult task of coordinating all agencies. I have noted with assurance your deep sense of responsibility and integrity in presenting all facts precisely as they were conceived to be. Your straight-forward attitude in presenting the weather situations and forecasts, frequently under the most difficult conditions, permitted me to reach decisions with confidence that I was acting on the best information and advice obtainable. This service on your part, and on the part of those associated with you, merits very special commendation as an outstanding contribution to the success of the whole operation. (Signed) Dwight D. Eisenhower DWIGHT D. EISENHOWER General, U.S. Army Letter from Dwight Eisenhower to James Stagg. Catalogue reference: AIR 73/8 After the war Stagg returned to the Met Office. In 1971 he published Forecast for Overlord, in which he gave his account of D-Day. He died on 23 June 1975 at the age of 74. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection The story of The Battle of Cable Street In 1936, Cable Street in London’s East End became the site of violent clashes between the British Union of Fascists and anti-fascist demonstrators. For many, this event symbolised community resistance to fascism, but what can archival records reveal about the realities behind this narrative? About this image Demonstrators at the junction of Aldgate and Commercial Road, from the Illustrated London News, 1936. On this page The road to Cable Street Opposition to the march 'They shall not pass' The aftermath of Cable Street Archives and collective memory Explore the records used in this story Important information ! This content discusses violence, antisemitism and discrimination. This material and related language is included to accurately reflect the past and the nature of our records. The road to Cable Street On Sunday 4 October 1936, a march through East London led by Oswald Mosley and the British Union of Fascists (BUF) was disrupted by anti-fascist counterdemonstrators. The BUF supported fascism, a far-right movement that believed some groups were superior to others. They also supported the use of violence against people who opposed their ideas. The BUF intended to parade through areas with significant Jewish populations but were stopped by a coalition of working men and women, Jewish people, dockers and immigrants. The Battle of Cable Street, as these events are often referred to, has developed an almost mythic status, representing the East End’s clear rejection of fascism. It is commemorated with a plaque and mural on walls along Cable Street. The Cable Street mural, found on St George’s Town Hall, Tower Hamlets. Photo taken by Simon Demissie. Records at The National Archives show a more nuanced picture. They indicate attempts to ban the fascist demonstration as well as advice from left wing and Jewish groups encouraging counterdemonstrators to avoid the march. Our records also show a spike in support for the BUF in East London in the immediate aftermath of The Battle of Cable Street. The BUF had developed a significant but notorious profile throughout the mid-1930s, even if it had failed to gather any electoral success, due to their extremist actions. For example, protestors at a BUF meeting in June 1934 were brutally beaten by the group. Additionally, street attacks on communists and Jewish people were committed regularly and continued until 1936. The BUF intended to celebrate this summer campaign on 4 October through a march and meetings in Shoreditch, Limehouse, Bow and Bethnal Green. Some of the group’s members openly declared that the march was a pogrom (targeted attack) on East London’s Jewish communities. Opposition to the march The upcoming march motivated action from the local community. In the week leading up to it a group of East End mayors firmly asked the Home Secretary Sir John Simon to ban it, with the Mayor of Stepney claiming that a march: …in this large Jewish populated area cannot but be provocative of disturbance and possible riot and danger to persons and property The Mayor of Stepney, 1936, Catalogue reference: HO 144/21060 Open transcript To THE RIGHT HON. SIR JOHN SIMON, P.C. H.M. Secretary for Home Affairs. WE, the undersigned citizens of East London, view with grave concern the proposed march of the British Union of Fascists upon East London. The avowed object of the Fascist movement in Great Britain is the incitement of malice and hatred against sections of the population. It aims to further ends which seek to destroy the harmony and goodwill which has existed for centuries among the East London population, irrespective of differences in race and creed. We consider racial incitement by a movement which employs flagrant distortion of truth and degrading calumny and vilification as a direct and deliberate provocation to malicious attack. We therefore make an earnest appeal to His Majesty's Secretary of State for Home Affairs, to prohibit such marches and thus retain peaceable and amicable relations between all sections of East London's population. Petition to Home Secretary Sir John Simon from Jewish residents of the East End. Catalogue reference: HO 144/21060 In the two days prior to the march the Jewish People’s Council collected an impressive 100,000 signatures to protest their ‘grave concern’. The petition expressed their fear that the ‘avowed object of the Fascist movement in Great Britain is the incitement of malice and hatred against sections of the population’. The petition ultimately asked the Home Secretary to prohibit such marches to unite and protect the community. Open transcript JEWISH PEOPLE’S COUNCIL AGAINST FASCISM AND ANTI-SEMITISM. NON POLITICAL 164 Commercial Road, E.1. 30th September 1936 The Right Hon. Sir John Simon, P.C. H.M. Secretary of State for Home Affairs. Dear Sir, The Jewish People’s Council is earnestly desirous for permission to have a deputation wait upon you in regard to the proposed British Union of Fascists march in East London on Sunday 4th October. As a large organisation with a specialised knowledge of conditions prevailing in East London at the moment (resultant upon recent Fascist agitation in the Area), we are most anxious to assist the Authorities in maintaining peace and order. We propose that our deputation be received by you on Friday, 2nd prox. at 11.30 a.m. when a petition supported by 100,000 signatures obtained within 2 days, expressing the feelings of East London’s population in the matter of the proposed march, will be presented. The deputation is in the position to support the petition by a reasoned statement, and it is our sincere hope, therefore, that in the interest of law and order you will accept the deputation from the Jewish People’s Council. The deputation will be led by James Hall, M.P. for Whitechapel and St. Georges, supported by A. M. Wall, Secretary of the London Trades Council, Father J. Groser of Christ Church, Watney Street, Stepney, E.1. and representatives of the Jewish People’s Council. Yours faithfully, J. Pearce Organising Secretary. Jewish People’s Council letter appealing for a meeting with Home Secretary Sir John Simon. Catalogue reference: HO 144/21060 Different publications took radically different positions in the days leading up to the march. The Jewish Chronicle issued a warning on the Saturday before the march urging Jewish people to keep away and going as far as to state: Jews who, however innocently, become involved in any possible disorders will be actively helping anti-Semitism and Jew-baiting. The Jewish Chronicle 'They shall not pass' The march went ahead with Sir Phillip Game, the Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, leading the policing of the event. The initial route was meant to see marchers’ parade down Commercial Street towards the East End. This was prevented by a huge crowd of anti-fascist demonstrators who blocked the intersection of Whitechapel High Street and Leman Street. A report in the Illustrated London News suggested a crowd of 100,000 counterdemonstrators was present. Although figures published at the time are now contested, they were significant and strongly outnumbers the fascists. Due to this the police advised a new route via Cable Street towards Stepney. On the new route, marchers continued to face pushback. On Cable Street, counterdemonstrators had overturned a brick-carrying truck to create a barricade. At the same time, they used the rallying cry ‘¡No pasarán!’ (meaning ‘they shall not pass’), which was commonly used by Spanish Republicans during this period. Stones and insults were also hurled, and Irish immigrant dockers who lived on the street joined in to stop the march moving forward. Following conversations between Game and Mosley, the fascists agreed to abandon the planned route and turned west towards the Embankment. Demonstrators at the junction of Aldgate and Commercial Road, from the Illustrated London News, 1936. Contrary to popular belief, much of the direct confrontation was not between the marchers and counterdemonstrators, but between the counterdemonstrators and the police. Children rolled marbles to make police horses fall over, and stones and insults were thrown towards the line of police officers trying to keep the two sides separated. This can be seen in an anonymised list of arrests which shows that of the 85 people arrested only six were fascists. The most common charges were insulting words and behaviour and obstructing police. A few were charged with the more serious crimes of grievous bodily harm and wilful damage. Interestingly, among the arrests were eight women and two children. The Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, Sir Phillip Game’s, account of the Battle of Cable Street Image 1 of 2 Page one of Sir Phillip Game’s account of the Battle of Cable Street. In this report, Game reports that he told Mosley, 'I am convinced that if you carry out your march and hold your meetings serious disorder is certain. I have therefore decided that neither the march nor the meetings can be allowed.' Catalogue reference: HO 144/21061 Image 2 of 2 Page two of Sir Phillip Game’s account of the Battle of Cable Street, including details on arrests. Catalogue reference: HO 144/21061 Previous Next Image 1 of 2 Image 2 of 2 The aftermath of Cable Street Despite the iconic status of these demonstrations as a triumph over fascism, in the wake of Cable Street the BUF’s membership increased. A report on the BUF notes that, by 27 October 1936, membership had increased by a little over 2,000. Most of these new members were from East End branches. Following the march and the violence of Cable Street, politicians and officials looked at ways to reduce the likelihood of similar events taking place again. The Public Order Bill was quickly developed, coming into law as The Public Order Act, in the beginning of January 1937. Among other things, the Act restricted the use of stewards at open air meetings and ensured that police had the power to ban marches or alter routes. It also outlawed the wearing of political uniforms. Among the banned uniforms were the black shirts of the British Union of Fascists. The BUF did not publicly disagree with the ruling, reiterating their ‘desire at all times to conform with the law of the land’ (catalogue reference: MEPO 3/2513). They did argue, however, that the police would not be able to ban the wearing of ‘an ordinary shirt of black colour with a black tie under an ordinary suit’. Open transcript British Union of Fascists and National Socialists Sanctuary Buildings, Great Smith Street, Westminster, S.W.1. 1 January, 1937. Sir, I thank you for your letter of the 31st December, and note that you are "not prepared to express an opinion" on the wearing of an ordinary shirt of black colour with a tie under an ordinary suit. I further note your statement that a Blackshirt is a "garment which has for some time past symbolised association with a political organisation" and beg to point out that the word employed in the Act is not "garment" but "uniform" and that on the legal interpretation of the latter word the whole issue rests. Pursuant to the advice in your letter of the 24th December we advised our members to discontinue wearing the Blackshirt uniform. Before advising them to adopt any distinctive mark which might show adherence to our Organisation we sought your opinion upon the legality of wearing an ordinary shirt of black colour with a tie under an ordinary suit. We need not remind you that such shirts can be bought in any shop, and have been worn for long past by some members of the public in no way associated with this organisation. We sought your opinion in order to prevent what might prove to be a widespread infringement of the law should the Courts later hold that such a shirt was in fact a uniform and, therefore, illegal. The fact that you did not see your way to give an opinion made it necessary for us to transmit our Counsel's advice to our members and leaves the responsibility for any infringement of the law upon the Home Office. Yours faithfully, N. Francis-Hawkins Director General of Organisation To: Commissioner of Police, New Scotland Yard, S.W.1. Letter from the British Union of Fascists regarding black shirts. Catalogue reference: MEPO 3/2513 Archives and collective memory The Battle of Cable Street signifies an important point in inter-war British history, when far-right political extremism was confronted on the streets of East London. While some claim that the immediate success of the coalition of anti-fascists has been overstated, memories of the event carry their own importance. The archival evidence allows us to re-engage with historical events and investigate their nuances. However, it is local community action and activity that decides how those events are remembered. Menu Visit What’s on Explore the collection Help using the archive Education Professional guidance and services Search Shop Home Explore the collection Stories from the collection Record revealed Adrienne de Lafayette’s letter to her husband, Marquis de Lafayette This previously unknown letter from Adrienne de Lafayette to her husband, the famed General Marquis de Lafayette, reveals her unfailing love for him and support for his cause. Images Image 1 of 3 Adrienne de Lafayette's letter. Image 2 of 3 The full text of the letter. Transcript Translation Transcript A Bordeaux ce 5 7bre 1778 Je quitte demain Bordeaux, mon cher coeur, et je vais retrouver notre pauvre petite anastasie et la retrouver bien portante; me reunir a notre chere enfans le seul gage qui me reste de notre tendresse et a maman qui m’est (comme je vous l’ai dis tans de fois) tous les jours plus chere parceque tous les jours il semble quelle vous aime dadvantage. Croiriés vous, mon coeur, qu’avec de tels sujets de joye (ou pour mieux dire de consolation) et que je sens mieux que personne, j’eprouve quelque regres en quittans cette ville parcequ’on y parle sans cesse de vous, que ma chere amerique est le sujet de toutes les conversations et que surtous j’y ai recu de vos nouvelles qui me remplissens d’esperance, et enfin j’apprends aujourdhuy que M Destaing est arrive en amerique j’espere donc de vous revoir cette année mais de grace prenés pour votre retour toutes les precautions possibles songés que je vous aime que vous mavés jusqu’a presens rendu assés malheureuse par votre absence, et les dangers que vous avés couru, et ne vous exposés pas dans le moment que vous commenceres de travailler a mon bonheur. Adieu je taime plus mon coeur que le monde entier ne pourrais te cherir. Tous ce que vous aimé ce porte bien je vous ai ecris 6 ou 7 lettres a la fois. Pour aujourdhuy je suis si pressée que je ne vous en dirai pas advantage. Translation Bordeaux, 5 September 1778 I leave Bordeaux tomorrow, my dear heart, to meet again with our poor little Anastasie and to find her well; to reunite with our dear child, the only token I have left of our tenderness, and my mother who is (as I told you many times) dearer to me every day as every day it seems that she loves you more. Would you believe, my heart, that with such causes for joy (or better said, for consolation) and that I feel better than anyone, I have some regrets in leaving this town because here they speak of you constantly, my dear America is the subject of all conversations and, above all, here I have received news from you which fill me with hope, and finally I have learned today that M. D’Estaing has arrived in America. I therefore hope to see you again this year, but please take all possible precautions for your return. Think about how I love you and how you have made me quite unhappy until now with your absence and the dangers you run into, and do not expose yourself at the moment you start working towards my happiness. Adieu I love you more, my heart, than the whole world ever could. All that you love is well. I wrote you six or seven letters. For today, I am in such a rush that I will say no more. Image 3 of 3 The letter's envelope. Transcript Translation Transcript A Monsieur Le Marquis de la Fayette General Major au service des Etas Unis de l’Amerique A l’armée Translation To Mr Marquis de la Fayette General Major in the service of the United States of America With the army Why this record matters Date 9 September 1778 Catalogue reference HCA 32/389/14 On 9 September 1778, Adrienne de Lafayette was preparing to return to Paris after a few months’ stay in Bordeaux. Amid the preparations, she hastily penned a short but affectionate letter to her husband, General Marquis de Lafayette. He was an ocean away fighting with the Continental Army against the British during the American Revolutionary War. Her letter, however, never reached her husband. The ship carrying Adrienne’s letter was captured by a British privateer (a private vessel commissioned by a government to attack enemy ships) off the coast of Virginia and brought into the Britain's vice-Admiralty Court in New York to be claimed as a prize. Prize-taking (the capture of enemies’ ships) was a normal practice of warfare at the time, but to ensure that a capture was legal, the captors had to bring their prizes before a court. Part of the legal process involved confiscating all documents on board. Due to this, Adrienne’s letter found its way into the High Court of Admiralty records now held at The National Archives, where it was recently discovered as part of the Prize Papers Project. The letter dates from the early years of Adrienne and Gilbert de Lafayette’s marriage in 1774. This was a time marked by lengthy periods of separation as the latter enthusiastically embraced the cause of American independence. Lafayette first sailed for America on the ship Victoire in April 1777, leaving behind his wife, then pregnant with their second child. Upon his arrival, he became a protégé of George Washington, who was general of the Continental Army and later the first president of the United States. Lafayette first saw action at the Battle of Brandywine in September 1777 and would play a prominent role throughout the American Revolutionary War. Lafayette’s military feats made him the main figure of France’s support for the American cause. Adrienne supported her husband’s endeavour, led by her devotion to him and her own ideals of liberty. In her letter, she writes of her sadness at leaving Bordeaux, where her husband and her ‘dear America’ were the main topics of conversation. As host to the first consulate of the United States, Bordeaux was a hub of supporters of the American cause. She clearly longed to see her husband again after more than a year of separation marked by personal tragedy. Their first child, Henriette, had died in the spring of 1778. Her death is evoked in the opening of the letter as Adrienne expresses her joy at soon reuniting with their daughter Anastasie, the ‘only token I have left of our tenderness’. Anastasie had stayed in Paris with her grandparents. Hoping to see him again in the new year, she urged him to take all necessary precautions for his safety: ‘Think about how I love you and how you have made me quite unhappy until now with your absence and the dangers you run into’. Adrienne would not have to wait long. He returned home in February 1779, acclaimed as a hero by the French public. Their son was born nine months later and named George Washington, a symbol of the couple’s connection with America that would last a lifetime.
